::: {#panel-methods .gw-tabpanel role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab-methods" tabindex="0"}

### The research question

How do local agencies account for interconnected water systems, track water
under land use alternatives, and involve communities?

Under SGMA an agency must define what unsustainable looks like, measure whether
it is happening, and act when it is. This analysis asks a narrower question of
each step: **which number actually becomes the quantity a decision is made on?**
It also asks what happens to the more sophisticated numbers that do not.

### Why these subbasins

{{< var basin_list >}} were selected for contrast rather than representativeness. They span the Sacramento Valley, the San Joaquin Valley and the Central Coast. They also differ in plan structure:

- one joint GSP (Merced, Turlock, Colusa);
- three GSPs under a coordination agreement (Kaweah);
- one GSP adopted by partner agencies (Salinas Valley);
- a single GSA (Yolo).

Four are covered by a Department of Conservation MLRP block grant. Colusa and Yolo are not. These differences are what make the comparison informative.

### Document collection and desktop review

For each subbasin the review assembled the adopted Groundwater Sustainability
Plan and any amendments, the most recent periodic evaluation and annual report,
GSA rules and regulations, land repurposing program instruments, technical
memoranda and ISW studies, relevant GSP appendices, agency correspondence, and
public comment letters.

### Literature review

{{< var literature_total >}} papers were reviewed across three topical areas:
groundwater accounting methods, land-use alternatives, and community
considerations. Each was assessed for the **method it demonstrates**, not for
its conclusions. That means what it measured, at what scale, using what data,
and whether an operational crediting or accounting program was involved.

### Coding and classification

Each finding was recorded with its subbasin, agency, document, chapter,
section, and the specific question it answers, together with a verbatim
quotation and the section or page it came from. Findings were classified as
**positive**, **absence**, or **ambiguous**, and rated for relevance to a
groundwater accounting platform and to DWR recommendations.

Extraction was AI-assisted. The analyst then checked quotations against the source documents for every subbasin, and {{< var quotes_verified >}} are marked verified. The analyst wrote the synthesis and key findings from the coded findings. The **Use of AI** tab explains each step.

### Cross-basin comparison

The same outline of chapters, sections and questions was put to each subbasin's document set. The cross-basin synthesis then works topic by topic. It covers what the literature says, what each subbasin's documents say (with document and page citations), a comparison across subbasins, and the gap the topic surfaces. The chapter pages present that synthesis directly. The key findings distil it.

**No maturity score, traffic light, or ranking is assigned anywhere on this
site.** There is one ordinal scale: the measurement states in the land
repurposing matrix. It describes how far quantification reaches for a benefit,
as rated by the analyst. It does not describe how good a program is.

### How to read an absence

The most important distinction in this analysis is between *not found in the
reviewed documents* and *does not exist*. An absence finding records the first.
It can arise for at least four reasons, and the site keeps them apart:

- the practice is genuinely absent from a document set that is otherwise complete;
- the relevant document was not available to review;
- the program exists but has not yet produced results;
- the question was never coded for that basin. This is a statement about the
  analysis, not about the basin.

:::
:::
:::

### What evidence is actually in scope

The site draws on {{< var active_streams >}} evidence streams. The key findings and cross-basin comparisons are based on the policy and planning documents and the academic literature. GSA board-meeting findings from WaterOne are a newer, separate collection. They can be explored on the Explore Findings page but have not yet been worked into the chapter conclusions.

:::

{{< include _partials/evidence_streams.html >}}

::: gw-prose

#### How meeting evidence is kept separate

Meeting findings record what was said in a board or committee meeting. That is
not what an agency adopted. They have their own tab, their own labels and
their own citations: the meeting body, date, agenda item and speaker role,
with a link to the WaterOne recap where one is supplied. They are not counted
in the site's statistics. Findings from subbasins outside the six case studies
are included for context and are not part of the cross-basin analysis.

:::
:::
:::

::: {#panel-limitations .gw-tabpanel role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab-limitations" tabindex="0" hidden="hidden"}
::: {.gw-page .gw-section .gw-section--tight}
::: gw-prose

### What this analysis cannot support

#### The document sets are not equally complete

This limitation matters most because it is the easiest to misread as a
finding. Some absences recorded for one subbasin are gaps in document
*availability*. For example, an MLRP plan, a siting-tool specification, and a
demand-management framework were not available to review. Other absences
reflect *architecture that has not yet produced results*. Examples include no
projects implemented, a monitoring plan still in draft, or a program plan not
yet final.

An absence tested against a rule in force is a much stronger finding than an
absence recorded against a program that has not started. The site preserves
that difference. A reader comparing cells across a row should too.

#### Comparisons cover different numbers of basins

Not every topic applies to every subbasin. Colusa and Yolo hold no MLRP grant, so most land repurposing topics compare four basins. Several community comparisons cover fewer. The equivalent instruments, such as a rulebook, a comment-response matrix, or a periodic evaluation, were not available for every basin. Where a basin is not covered, the site says so rather than treating it as an absence.

#### This is a desktop analysis

Findings describe what the reviewed documents say. No interviews were
conducted, no agency staff were asked to confirm or correct an interpretation,
and no independent measurement was made. A practice that exists but is not
documented in the reviewed material would appear here as an absence.

#### The evidence is a point in time

Documents were reviewed as they stood in mid-2026. Plans are amended, annual
reports are published, monitoring networks change, and grant programs end.
Several findings here depend on facts that are explicitly dated.

#### Spatial data is not part of this analysis

No geographic analysis was performed. The map uses public DWR and USGS
layers for orientation only. Land repurposing project locations in particular
are documented inconsistently across the subbasins, which is itself recorded
as a limitation rather than smoothed over.

:::
:::
:::

### How AI was used in this project

AI tools supported three parts of this project: extracting findings from
documents, building the website, and drafting site copy. The analytical
judgments were made by the analyst. This tab describes where AI was used and
how its output was checked.

#### Finding extraction

A language model was given the question outline and each subbasin's documents.
It was instructed to answer each question with a direct quotation and a
citation to the document and section or page. This produced the first draft
of the coded findings.

#### Verification by the analyst

The analyst checked quotations against the source documents for every
subbasin. {{< var quotes_verified >}} of {{< var findings_total >}} findings
are marked verified. A verified quotation is accurate to its source. Whether
it fully answers the question it is attached to was reviewed, but is not
guaranteed for every row.

#### Synthesis and conclusions

The cross-basin synthesis, the key findings, and the implications for the
Groundwater Accounting Platform and DWR were written by the analyst from the
coded findings.

#### Building this website

The site was designed and built with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code)
working under the author's direction. It wrote the data-processing scripts,
the interactive explorers and the web graphics. The author reviewed the
output, set the design direction, and decided what each page should say.

#### Drafting site copy

Some page copy was drafted with AI assistance from the synthesis report and
then edited by the author. Direct quotations are never generated. Every
quotation on the site is copied exactly from the coding workbooks or the WaterOne export.

#### Safeguards built into the site

- Every count on the site is computed from the processed data at build time.
- Quotations and source locations are carried over from the source files without
  rewording.
- Absence findings always read "not found in reviewed documents."
- No score, rating or category is assigned unless it is recorded in the
  source materials.

:::
:::
:::

### Project role

This site is an independent portfolio adaptation of a landscape analysis
conducted for the California Department of Water Resources Groundwater
Accounting project. The underlying cross-basin synthesis and the coded findings
database are the author's own work within that project.

The work covered:

- desktop review of Groundwater Sustainability Plans, amendments, periodic
  evaluations, annual reports, GSA rules, land repurposing program instruments,
  technical studies, and public comment letters across
  {{< var active_basins >}} subbasins;
- a review of {{< var literature_total >}} academic papers across groundwater
  accounting methods, land-use alternatives, and community considerations;
- structured coding and classification of {{< var findings_total >}} findings,
  including verbatim quotation capture and verification against source
  documents;
- cross-basin comparison and synthesis;
- identification of implications for a groundwater accounting platform and for
  DWR recommendations;
- design and development of this public interactive adaptation.

::: {.gw-callout}
<p class="gw-callout__label">Attribution</p>

This is a portfolio project. It is not a DWR publication, does not carry DWR
branding, and its interpretations are the author's own. Where the analysis was
conducted as part of a wider project team, the site does not claim sole
authorship of that project's work.
:::

### Illustration credits

New diagrams on this site are original responsive web graphics built for this
adaptation.

::: {.gw-callout .gw-callout--placeholder}
<p class="gw-callout__label">Reserved for authorized illustrations</p>

Selected graphics from *Well, Well, Well: An Introduction to Groundwater
Recovery* by Sara Soroka and Travis Rennacker may be reused here with
permission. **No such illustration is currently in use on this site.** When
assets are supplied, each will carry a figure-level credit and be listed here
in the form:

> Illustration by Sara Soroka. Originally created for *Well, Well, Well: An
> Introduction to Groundwater Recovery* by Sara Soroka and Travis Rennacker.
> Used with permission.
:::

### Sources and tools

The analysis is based on publicly available planning and policy documents
published by the groundwater sustainability agencies named throughout, and on
published academic literature. This site is a static Quarto website. All
filtering and search happen in the browser, using data processed from the
coding workbooks at build time.

### Photography

Chapter photographs are from [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com) and are used
under the Pexels license. Each carries a credit line beneath it.

```{=html}
<script>
/* Tab panels. Full keyboard support: arrow keys move between tabs, Home and
   End jump to the ends, and the selected panel is the only one in the
   accessibility tree. Panels are plain sections, so a direct link such as
   methods.html#limitations still reveals the right one. */
(function () {
  var tablist = document.querySelector('.gw-tabs');
  if (!tablist) return;
  var tabs = Array.prototype.slice.call(tablist.querySelectorAll('[role="tab"]'));

  function select(tab, focus) {
    tabs.forEach(function (t) {
      var panel = document.getElementById(t.getAttribute('aria-controls'));
      var on = t === tab;
      t.setAttribute('aria-selected', on ? 'true' : 'false');
      t.setAttribute('tabindex', on ? '0' : '-1');
      if (panel) panel.hidden = !on;
    });
    if (focus) tab.focus();
    history.replaceState(null, '', '#' + tab.getAttribute('aria-controls').replace('panel-', ''));
  }

  tabs.forEach(function (tab, i) {
    tab.setAttribute('tabindex', tab.getAttribute('aria-selected') === 'true' ? '0' : '-1');
    tab.addEventListener('click', function () { select(tab, false); });
    tab.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
      var next = null;
      if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') next = tabs[(i + 1) % tabs.length];
      else if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft') next = tabs[(i - 1 + tabs.length) % tabs.length];
      else if (e.key === 'Home') next = tabs[0];
      else if (e.key === 'End') next = tabs[tabs.length - 1];
      if (next) { e.preventDefault(); select(next, true); }
    });
  });

  /* Deep links: #literature, #panel-literature, or a fragment inside a panel. */
  function openFromHash() {
    var hash = window.location.hash.slice(1);
    if (!hash) return;
    var target = document.getElementById('panel-' + hash) || document.getElementById(hash);
    if (!target) return;
    var panel = target.closest ? target.closest('.gw-tabpanel') : null;
    if (!panel) return;
    var tab = document.getElementById(panel.id.replace('panel-', 'tab-'));
    if (tab) select(tab, false);
  }
  openFromHash();
  window.addEventListener('hashchange', openFromHash);
})();
</script>
</main>
```
